title: Twenty years after Hines, Hungerford, and Tomera: A new meta-analysis of psycho-social determinants of pro-environmental behaviour
review_question: To replicate and extend the Hines et al. (1986/87) meta-analysis on psycho-social determinants of pro-environmental behaviour by pooling bivariate correlations and testing an integrative theoretical model using meta-analytic structural equation modeling (MASEM).
inclusion_exclusion_criteria: Studies published since 1995 in peer-reviewed journals, applying NAM, TPB, or similar models; analyzing at least two constructs from the theoretical model; having construct definitions/measures fitting the authors' understanding; and reporting bivariate Pearson correlations and sample size.

findings.quote: Based on 17 studies we found a random-effects mean correlation of r = .42 between attitude and pro-environmental behaviour.
For the association of PBC and pro-environmental behaviour we found a mean correlation of r = .30 (18 studies).
We found a mean correlation of moral norm and pro-environmental behaviour of r = .39 (11 studies).
In our meta-analysis, the mean correlation of intention and pro-environmental behaviour is r = .52 (15 studies).

synthesis_conclusions: Behavioural intention mediates the impact of all other psycho-social variables on pro-environmental behaviour, explaining 27% of its variance.
Perceived behavioural control (PBC), attitude, and moral norm are significant independent predictors of intention, collectively explaining 52% of its variance.
Problem awareness, internal attribution, feelings of guilt, and social norms significantly contribute to the prediction of moral norm, explaining 58% of its variance.
Pro-environmental behaviour is best viewed as a mixture of self-interest and pro-social motives, both of which are accounted for by the integrative model.
The meta-analysis results for pooled mean correlations are very similar to those reported by Hines et al. (1986/87), indicating high temporal stability of these associations.
evidence_gaps: Lack of systematic research on the association between internal attribution processes, feelings of guilt, pro-environmental social norms, and attitudes.
Need for more research on the role of 'moral' emotions (empathic distress, guilt, shame) in the formation and activation of pro-environmental moral norms.
Potential influence of cultural differences on construct associations and the relevance of self-interest vs. pro-social motives.
Processes contributing to the actual enactment of pro-environmental behavioural intention are not fully understood (e.g., implementation intention, habit).
Future research should focus more on direct experimental tests of causal processes rather than correlational studies.
risk_of_bias_assessment: Funnel plots were used for a graphical 'eyeball' test. The plot for intention-behaviour correlations showed a 'hole' in the low left part, suggesting a potential bias from not reporting low, insignificant intention-behaviour correlations.
heterogeneity_sources: Statistical tests (Q-statistic) indicated strong heterogeneity for most pooled correlations (30 out of 32).
Associations of model constructs vary considerably across the type of pro-environmental behaviour or the kind of sample analysed in primary studies.
publication_bias: Possible overestimation of the intention-behaviour correlation due to reporting bias (file drawer problem), as suggested by the funnel plot analysis.
limitations: Low total number of available studies restricts conducting moderator analyses.
MASEM methodological problems: determination of appropriate sample size (harmonic mean of n=1341 is an ad hoc solution, not based on statistical theory).
MASEM based on univariate-z pooled correlations ignores sampling variation across studies and potential covariation among elements of the pooled correlation matrix.
MASEM uses a correlation matrix instead of a covariance matrix as input, which may lead to incorrect chi-square statistics and standard errors of parameter estimation.
Correlational tests do not allow causal inferences.
